newsitem.title: PERU: Explosions in night break edgy peace in Peru siege. [CORRECTED 00:05 08/01]
newsitem.headline: Explosions in night break edgy peace in Peru siege. [CORRECTED 00:05 08/01]

text.p: Two explosions punctuated the stalemate in Peru's hostage crisis on Tuesday, shattering an edgy peace at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence where Marxist rebels hold 74 captives.

As the deadlocked crisis ended its third week (corrects from "entered it's third week"), two loud booms -- assumed to be gunshots -- rang out shortly before dawn, immediately followed by silence. Witnesses said they believed two Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) members had slipped out of the building toward cars in the driveway, then fired a warning salvo as they went back inside.

Reuters Television images filmed from a vantage point above the residence showed a man dressed in combat gear and carrying an automatic rifle running across the driveway at the front of the compound shortly before the explosions.

"I saw two of them. They ran back at different times," Reuters cameraman Carlos Valdez said. "I think the guerrillas were trying to get one of the car batteries but they made a noise and decided to abort the operation, firing a couple of shots after they reached the house again."
Police surrounding the residence could not confirm that version of events but immediately moved to a state of alert. They speculated the MRTA was trying to make its presence felt.
"We think it was a psychological tactic to let us know that they're there," one policeman said.

The explosions were the first heard at the residence since Dec. 26, when a single loud boom briefly shook the area. That explosion was believed to be caused by an animal tripping a mine in the compound.

The explosions underscored the delicately balanced nature of the crisis, which began 21 days ago when about 20 heavily armed MRTA rebels stormed a coktail party at the residence and took more than 500 guests hostage.

President Alberto Fujimori, who has maintained a "no compromise" stand throughout the siege, met late into the night with ministers to discuss options for a peaceful end to the crisis, Government Palace sources said. The meeting lasted nearly 10 hours.

Fujimori has rejected rebel demands that he free about 400 of their imprisoned comrades. In a hard-hitting speech last week, he called the MRTA "terrorists" bent on pointless violence that served to increase poverty in Peru.
The rebels have not freed any hostages since that speech, and an MRTA spokesman said on Monday they would continue to hold firm until the two sides sat down to negotiate.

"There will be no more releases so long as the government fails to agree to a political solution," Isaac Velazco, the MRTA's international spokesman, said in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.

He said a "political solution" would consist of Fujimori sending Education Minister Domingo Palermo for further talks inside the residence and allowing rebels to communicate with their imprisoned comrades.

Palermo, Fujimori's chief negotiator, held face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA on Dec. 28. The meeting was followed by the release of 20 hostages and a conciliatory rebel statement expressing willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."

But Palermo has not been sent back to the residence and the rebels have hardened their position. "We have made too many gestures. We have released many people without receiving a single response from the government," Velazco said.

The series of hostage releases in which the guerrillas have freed a total of more than 430 captives has stopped since seven were let out on New Year's Day. The impasse has sparked fears that one false move by the government or rebels could trigger a bloody showdown.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned on Monday that the situation could get out of hand. "It will be a protracted battle and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," he told reporters.
The rebels, who possess automatic rifles and grenade launchers, have mined and booby-trapped the residence in anticipation of an assault by government forces.

Fujimori's ex-wife, Susana Higuchi, warned him in an interview published on Tuesday not to negotiate with the rebels. "They are a bunch of criminals and killers involved in the drug trade and there is nothing to negotiate with them," the former first lady, who divorced Fujimori in 1995, told the Argentine newspaper La Nacion.
